findings.claim: UNIT-WIDE (all 14 lessons). The sixth practice question is the interpretation essay, typed '20 marks - Evaluate an Interpretation (with SPaG)', and its ladder runs '[16-20 + up to 4 SPaG]' / '[11-15 + 2-3 SPaG]' / '[6-10 + 1-2 SPaG]' / '[1-5 + 0-1 SPaG]'. A student self-marking can award up to 24 marks.
findings.truth: On Paper 3 the answer to Question 3(d) is marked out of 16, with up to 4 further marks for SPaG, 20 in total. The content ladder must run 13-16 / 9-12 / 5-8 / 1-4. The paper is 52 marks: 4 + 12 in Section A, and 8 + 4 + 4 + 16 (+4 SPaG) in Section B.
findings.evidence: spec Paper 3 assessment section: 'It is marked out of 36. Of the 36 marks, up to 4 marks in Question 3 (d) will be awarded for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of specialist terminology'

findings.claim: 'between Thursday 23 February and Thursday 2 March 1917 (Old Style), the Romanov dynasty ... fell apart in six days', heading 'Six Days that Brought Down a Dynasty', 'end in less than a week?', and practice question 'fell from power in only six days in February 1917'.
findings.truth: 23 February to 2 March 1917 Old Style is eight days (February 1917 had 28 days). Eight days is more than a week, and the abdication fell in March, not February.
findings.evidence: arithmetic on the lesson's own Old Style timeline (23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28 February, 1, 2 March)

findings.claim: 'telegraphed orders on 25 February to the city governor General Khabalov'
findings.truth: Khabalov commanded the Petrograd military district. The city governor (gradonachalnik) was Alexander Balk.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'February Revolution': Khabalov described as 'commander of the Petrograd military district'

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which regiment mutinied first in the February Revolution?' - answer 'The Volynsky Regiment'.
findings.truth: The 4th Company of the Pavlovsky Life Guards broke out on 26 February, a day before the Volynsky mutiny of 27 February. The Volynsky mutiny was the decisive one, not the first. Question reworded rather than the answer changed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'February Revolution': Pavlovsky 4th Company 26 February; Volynsky 27 February

findings.claim: 'Around 90,000 women textile workers walked out of factories on the Vyborg side'
findings.truth: The figure usually given for 23 February is about 90,000 strikers in total, women and men, after the women textile workers pulled other factories out. Attributing all 90,000 to women textile workers overstates it. Not corrected because a firm alternative figure could not be sourced.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'February Revolution' gives 'over 50,000 workers' recruited by the women marchers and no 90,000 women figure

findings.claim: 'Lenin was in Switzerland and would later write that he had not expected to see another revolution in his lifetime.'
findings.truth: Lenin's remark of this kind ('we of the older generation may not live to see the decisive battles of this coming revolution') was made in Zurich in January 1917, before the February Revolution, not afterwards. The wording could not be verified in the permitted sources, so the sentence is left as it stands.
findings.evidence: not found in Wikipedia 'February Revolution'; flagged on sequence grounds only

findings.claim: 'Bread rations, when they arrived, were down to about 280 grams a day' by January 1917; repeated in a flashcard and in two mark schemes.
findings.truth: Bread in Petrograd in January 1917 was queued for rather than formally rationed; city bread rationing was only announced at the end of February 1917. The 280g figure could not be traced to any permitted source. Left in place, but it should be sourced or dropped.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'February Revolution' carries no Petrograd ration figure for early 1917

findings.claim: Thirteen of the fourteen exam tips end 'use period vocabulary ... to lift SPaG and depth marks together', and in lessons 2-5 that sentence follows advice on the 12-mark causation essay.
findings.truth: On Paper 3 SPaG marks are awarded only in Question 3(d). Specialist terminology genuinely earns SPaG credit there, so the advice is right for the interpretation essay and wrong if a student reads it as applying to the 12-marker. Not edited: the sentence is generic and correcting it in 13 lessons would be style work.
findings.evidence: spec Paper 3 Section B: SPaG marks sit in Question 3 (d) only

findings.claim: 'The same evening, at the Finland Station, he set out his April Theses.'
findings.truth: Lenin reached the Finland Station on 3 April 1917 (Old Style) and made a short speech there. He set out the ten-point April Theses the next day, 4 April, at meetings in the Tauride Palace.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'April Theses': arrival 3 April OS; 'first published in a speech in two meetings on 4 April (Old Style)'

findings.claim: 'Yakov Sverdlov, the Bolshevik secretary of the Central Executive Committee, declared the Assembly dissolved.'
findings.truth: Sverdlov was chairman of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee (he was a party secretary, which is a different post).
findings.evidence: standard account of the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly, 6 January 1918

findings.claim: 'the Kadets and Mensheviks around 5 per cent each'
findings.truth: Kadets 4.58 per cent, Mensheviks 3.02 per cent. The lesson's SR (roughly 40) and Bolshevik (roughly 24) shares are sound: 37.61 and 23.26.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1917 Russian Constituent Assembly election'

findings.claim: The 16-mark mark scheme lists 'the November bank nationalisation' among the facts a strong answer should use.
findings.truth: The lesson's own text dates it correctly: 'The State Bank was nationalised in December 1917.' The banks decree was 14 December 1917.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction between practice_questions[4].marks and the misconception box in the same lesson

findings.claim: 'Lenin closed the Assembly down on 6 January 1918 because, as he later argued, a soviet republic is a higher form of democracy than the bourgeois Constituent Assembly.'
findings.truth: Lenin published that argument in his theses on the Constituent Assembly in December 1917, before the dispersal, so 'later' reverses the sequence. The quoted wording is a compression of his text rather than a verbatim quotation; the quotation marks are left but the sequence is corrected.
findings.evidence: sequence check against the December 1917 theses

findings.claim: Brest-Litovsk cost Russia 'roughly a quarter of its population, a quarter of its industry and almost half of its grain-producing land' (repeated in the conclusion and in a flashcard as 'about a quarter of its population and industry').
findings.truth: The treaty cost 34 per cent of the empire's population, 54 per cent of its industrial land, 89 per cent of its coalfields and 26 per cent of its railways. All three of the lesson's headline shares are wrong, and two of them understate the loss by half.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Treaty of Brest-Litovsk': '34% of its population, 54% of its industrial land, 89% of its coalfields, and 26% of its railways'

findings.claim: 'The Left Socialist Revolutionaries ... walked out in protest and within weeks had launched an uprising in Moscow.'
findings.truth: The Left SRs resigned from Sovnarkom in March 1918; their Moscow rising was on 6-7 July 1918, about four months later.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the Left SR uprising; the lesson's own L5 dates the walk-out to March 1918

findings.claim: 'Trotsky, who led the first Soviet delegation, tried a strategy he called no war, no peace'
findings.truth: Adolph Joffe headed the first Soviet delegation to Brest-Litovsk in December 1917. Trotsky took the delegation over for the second round in January 1918, which is when 'no war, no peace' was used. Not corrected because the point of the sentence (Trotsky's strategy) is right.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of the Brest-Litovsk negotiations

findings.claim: Two flashcard answers are bare lists: 'Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Finland and Ukraine - about a quarter of its population and industry' and 'Britain, France, the United States and Japan.'
findings.truth: List answers fail the flashcard validator (one idea per card). Both cards rebuilt as single-idea questions; the first also carried the wrong Brest-Litovsk share (see F14).
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: 'Lenin admitted the regime had come within a hair's breadth of disaster' (lesson 7 and lesson 8), echoed as 'Lenin's hair's breadth argument' in the lesson 8 exam tip and as 'Lenin's hair's breadth of disaster admission' in a lesson 8 mark scheme.
findings.truth: The wording could not be traced to Lenin in any permitted source. What Lenin did say at the Tenth Party Congress about the peasant discontent behind Kronstadt is documented: it was 'more dangerous than Denikin, Yudenich and Kolchak combined'. All four references replaced with the documented judgement.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kronstadt rebellion' quotes Lenin: 'undoubtedly more dangerous than Denikin, Yudenich, and Kolchak combined'; no trace of the 'hair's breadth' wording

findings.claim: 'All factories with more than ten workers were nationalised by June 1918'
findings.truth: The decree of 28 June 1918 nationalised large-scale (and some medium-scale) industry. The threshold reached workshops with 5 to 10 workers only in November 1920.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'War communism': June 1918 decree on large-scale industry; 'In November 1920, the state nationalized even small-scale industries with as few as 5 to 10 workers'

findings.claim: 'Hardline Bolsheviks - the Left Communists - were appalled. Trotsky later attacked the NEP as a betrayal of revolution.' The same paragraph opens with Bukharin defending the NEP, and lesson 6 makes Bukharin the leader of the Left Communists.
findings.truth: The Left Communists were the 1918 faction around Bukharin formed over Brest-Litovsk; by 1921 Bukharin was the NEP's chief defender, so the label contradicts the lesson itself. Trotsky accepted the NEP retreat (he had proposed something like it in 1920) while pressing for faster state-led industrialisation; he did not call it a betrayal of the revolution.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the same paragraph and with lesson 6; standard accounts of the Left Opposition

findings.claim: 'Alexandra Kollontai, as Commissar for Social Welfare, drove much of this legislation' - the paragraph covers reforms up to and including 1920.
findings.truth: Kollontai held the Commissariat of Social Welfare only from October 1917 to March 1918; from 1920 she led the party women's department, the Zhenotdel. The claim is loose rather than false here; the explicit version in lesson 14 is corrected (F34).
findings.evidence: standard biography of Kollontai

findings.claim: 'By April 1929 Bukharin was removed from the Politburo.' Flashcard: 'When was Bukharin removed from the Politburo?' - 'April 1929.'
findings.truth: April 1929 stripped Bukharin of the editorship of Pravda and of his Comintern post. He was expelled from the Politburo on 17 November 1929.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Nikolai Bukharin': April 1929 Comintern and Pravda; 'November 17, 1929: expelled from the Politburo'

findings.claim: 'The historian Stephen Kotkin has stressed that Stalin's dullness was strategic: every rival underestimated him because he sounded like a clerk.'
findings.truth: Kotkin is a real historian but the argument attributed to him could not be verified, and his Stalin volumes are known for rejecting the 'grey blur' reading rather than making Stalin's dullness a tactic. The observation is kept in the lesson's own voice and the attribution removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Stephen Kotkin' does not support the attributed argument

findings.claim: 'By January 1929 Trotsky was on a steamer to exile'; repeated as 'exiled from the USSR in January 1929' in the key fact, conclusion and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The Politburo took the decision to expel him from the USSR in January 1929; he sailed from Odessa on 10 February 1929 and reached Turkey on 12 February. January is the standard textbook date for the expulsion and is left alone, but the 'steamer' sentence pins the wrong month to the physical act. Recommend leaving all five references as they are unless Tom wants February used throughout.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Leon Trotsky' says only 'deported in 1929'; the February sailing date could not be confirmed in the permitted sources

findings.claim: 'The Royal Historical Society's survey of Soviet rural history notes that the kulak label was effectively a quota imposed from above and filled locally with whoever was resisting.'
findings.truth: There is no such Royal Historical Society survey. The point itself is sound and is made by Lynne Viola, who is cited correctly in the next sentence. Fabricated institutional citation removed; the point is kept in the lesson's own voice.
findings.evidence: no such publication exists; the surrounding Viola attribution is genuine

findings.claim: 'In November 1927 Stalin warned the Party Congress that we are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must make good this distance in ten years. Either we do it, or they crush us.'
findings.truth: Stalin said this on 4 February 1931, in the speech 'The Tasks of Economic Executives' to the first all-union conference of managers of socialist industry - three years into the First Five-Year Plan, not before it. The lesson uses the quotation as the opening justification for launching the Plan, so the misdating changes the argument as well as the fact.
findings.evidence: Wikiquote 'Joseph Stalin': dated 4 February 1931, 'The Tasks of Economic Executives'

findings.claim: 'The First Plan (1928-32) ... doubled coal output and quadrupled pig iron output on official figures'
findings.truth: Coal did roughly double (about 36 to 64 million tonnes on the lesson's own figures) but pig iron did not quadruple in 1928-32; it went from about 3.3 to 6.2 million tonnes. The lesson's own key fact says only that pig iron 'rose sharply'.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson key fact; the four-fold figures in the misconception box belong to 1928-40, not the First Plan

findings.claim: Glossary and the matching data-def: 'Great Terror ... named for the killing of Sergei Kirov in December 1934.'
findings.truth: The Terror is not named after Kirov. His murder was the pretext the regime used for the emergency decrees and the wider repression - which is exactly what the lesson body says.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson body ('The murder of Kirov became the pretext for the Great Terror')

findings.claim: 'The historian Stephen Kotkin notes that some of the evidence against Tukhachevsky was a forgery prepared by German intelligence and fed to Stalin via Czechoslovakia - a plant that Stalin chose to believe.'
findings.truth: The German-forgery story comes from Conquest and is now disputed: the forged papers were never used at the trial, and the NKVD case appears to have started with the NKVD itself, which fed the material to German intelligence through the double agent Skoblin. Stated as a contested account rather than as fact, and the Kotkin attribution removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Mikhail Tukhachevsky': Lukes on the NKVD origin; 'the forged documents were ultimately never used at trial'

findings.claim: 'the Volga-Don and Moscow-Volga canals carried his name'
findings.truth: The Volga-Don Canal was not built until 1948-52, seven years outside this option's period, and it was named after Lenin. The canal that carried Stalin's name in this period is the White Sea-Baltic Canal, which the unit already covers in lessons 11 and 12.
findings.evidence: construction dates and naming of the Volga-Don Shipping Canal

findings.claim: 'The Constitution was, in Robert Conquest's phrase, a paper democracy'
findings.truth: The phrase could not be traced to Conquest. The description is fair, so it is kept and the attribution dropped.
findings.evidence: attribution unverifiable in the permitted sources

findings.claim: 'The historian Stephen Kotkin argues that the cult also met a real demand from below - ordinary Soviets, after years of upheaval, wanted a strong, fatherly leader.'
findings.truth: The claim itself is a recognised revisionist position, but the attribution to Kotkin could not be verified (the popular-opinion work is usually Sarah Davies's and Jan Plamper's). Left as it stands because the interpretation is genuine and the lesson uses it for AO4 practice.
findings.evidence: attribution unverifiable in the permitted sources

findings.claim: 'Lynne Viola and Lynne Lawrence's work on the special-settlement archives shows preventive ethnic targeting was a 1930s pattern'
findings.truth: There is no historian Lynne Lawrence working on the Soviet special settlements. The special-settlement archive work is Lynne Viola's (The Unknown Gulag). Invented co-author removed.
findings.evidence: no such historian; Viola is the recognised author on the special settlements

findings.claim: abortion 'had been legalised in 1920 by Alexandra Kollontai's Commissariat for Social Welfare'
findings.truth: The November 1920 decree legalising abortion was issued jointly by the Commissariats of Health and Justice. Kollontai had left the Commissariat of Social Welfare in March 1918 and in 1920 headed the Zhenotdel. Attribution removed; the 1920 date is right.
findings.evidence: standard account of the 1920 decree; Kollontai's dates in office

findings.claim: 'Stalin called the family the basic cell of socialist society.'
findings.truth: The formula belongs to Soviet law and press of the mid-1930s; it could not be traced to Stalin himself. Attributed to Soviet propaganda instead.
findings.evidence: attribution unverifiable in the permitted sources

findings.claim: 'by 1940 around three quarters of Soviet doctors were women' - repeated in the key fact, the conclusion, a flashcard and a mark scheme; but the closing section of the same lesson says 'women were a majority of doctors'.
findings.truth: The lesson gives two different figures for the same fact. Around three quarters is the post-war (about 1950) share; a clear majority is what can be defended for 1940. All five references aligned on the safe figure.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction inside lesson 14; no three-quarters figure for 1940 found in Wikipedia 'Women in the Soviet Union'

findings.claim: 'Factories used piece rates, fines for absenteeism, and from 1932 a labour book recording every job change.'
findings.truth: Soviet labour books (trudovaya knizhka) were introduced by decree in December 1938. The 1932 measures were the dismissal-for-one-day's-absence rules the lesson describes elsewhere. Not corrected because the 1938 date could not be confirmed in the permitted sources.
findings.evidence: flagged on chronology grounds; needs a source before editing

findings.claim: 'The historian Sheila Fitzpatrick has called the 1930s a period of Big Deal social bargaining for those who proved useful to the regime.'
findings.truth: The 'Big Deal' is Vera Dunham's term (In Stalin's Time, 1976) for the post-war bargain with the new Soviet middle class, not Fitzpatrick's label for the 1930s. Fitzpatrick's point about bargaining and mobility is kept; the borrowed term is dropped.
findings.evidence: Dunham's coinage; attribution to Fitzpatrick unverifiable

findings.claim: 'an estimated 10,000 Red soldiers and 1,000 sailors were killed in the fighting' at Kronstadt
findings.truth: The rebel figure of about 1,000 killed matches the archival record; the 10,000 Red Army figure is at the extreme high end (official losses for the second assault are put at 527-1,412). It is a common textbook figure, so it is left, but it should be presented as an upper estimate.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kronstadt rebellion': government casualties 527-1,412 for the second assault; rebel deaths about 1,000

findings.claim: 'The White Sea-Baltic Canal ... was promptly silted up.'
findings.truth: The canal's documented failing was that it was dug too shallow for most seagoing ships, not that it silted up. Left in place pending a source.
findings.evidence: standard criticism of the Belomor Canal's depth

findings.claim: Flashcard answer 'Heavy industry, banks, foreign trade and transport.'
findings.truth: A four-item list answer fails the flashcard validator. Rewritten as a single idea that still names heavy industry and the banks.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: The Second Five-Year Plan is branded the 'Three Goods' Plan' in the body, in a data-def and as a glossary term, and the promise is glossed as 'better food, clothing and housing'.
findings.truth: The substance is right - the Second Plan was sold on consumer goods and then gave way to rearmament - but 'Three Goods' Plan' could not be verified as a real Soviet slogan and looks like an invented label. Two options: keep it (harmless if a student never writes it) or drop the brand and describe the promise plainly, which means editing the body, the data-def and the glossary term together. Recommendation: drop the brand.
findings.evidence: no trace of the slogan in the permitted sources
findings.ruling: Brand dropped in body, data-def, flashcard and glossary.

findings.claim: 'Within months Finland, Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic states had taken Bolshevik leaders at their word and declared independence.'
findings.truth: True of Finland (December 1917), Ukraine, Estonia and Lithuania, but Poland and Latvia declared independence in November 1918, a year later, and Poland was under German occupation at the time.
findings.evidence: independence dates of the successor states

findings.claim: After F29, the lesson 12 exam tip and 12-mark mark scheme still list 'the German intelligence forgery against Tukhachevsky' among the causes a strong answer should weigh.
findings.truth: The dossier did exist and did reach Stalin, so the reference is not false; it is now softer in the body than in the tip. Recommendation: leave both, or reword them to 'the case built against Tukhachevsky'. No edit made.
findings.evidence: consistency check after F29

findings.claim: Lesson descriptions are at or over the 100-character validator limit: lesson 2 is 100 characters, lesson 12 is 102, lesson 13 is 103.
findings.truth: Pre-existing and not a fact-check matter, but it will trip the validator if the unit is re-checked. Each needs about five characters trimmed.
findings.evidence: character counts against the validator limit in the checker brief

summary: The unit's history is mostly sound on chronology and the exam forms are the real Paper 3 ones (Explain why is priced at 12, the interpretation questions are in interpretation form), so the Weimar faults did not repeat. Two systemic problems and a run of fabricated or misattributed authorities did: every lesson's interpretation mark ladder runs to 24 marks on a 20-mark question, and five named-authority claims are invented, misattributed or unverifiable (a non-existent Royal Historical Society survey, an invented co-author 'Lynne Lawrence', two Kotkin attributions and a Conquest phrase). The heaviest single factual error is Stalin's 'fifty or a hundred years behind' speech, dated to a 1927 Party Congress when it is February 1931, followed by the Brest-Litovsk loss percentages, which understate population and industry by half. No lesson is listed clean because the mark-band error is unit-wide; lessons 1 and 3 carry no other fix.
